title: Pronouns and address
matching: Typed answers ignore letter case, extra spaces, apostrophe style and final . ! or ? punctuation. Accents and every other character count. Multiple-choice answers must match exactly.

lessons.title: Forms of address: você, tu, a gente and o senhor/a senhora
lessons.explanation: Você takes the same verb form as ele/ela (você fala, você come) and is the neutral word for 'you' across most of Brazil. Tu is used in parts of the country, in some regions with the ele form (tu fala) and in others with the standard tu form (tu falas). Learn to recognise it, and use você unless you live where tu is normal. A gente means 'we' in speech and takes the ele form: A gente vai ao cinema. Nós is more formal. O senhor and a senhora are formal and polite, with the ele form: O senhor quer um café? Vocês is the plural of você and tu, with the eles form.

examples.en: Do you live near here?

examples.pt: A gente vai ao cinema hoje.
examples.en: We are going to the cinema today.
Would you like a coffee, madam?

lessons.title: Direct object pronouns: o, a, os, as and Brazilian ele/ela
lessons.explanation: The direct object pronouns are o, a, os, as (him/it, her/it, them). They replace the noun that receives the verb: Vi o filme becomes Vi-o or, in formal writing, Eu o vi. Brazilian speech very often uses ele or ela as the object instead: Eu vi ele. Both are understood, but o/a is the correct written form. When the verb ends in -r, -s or -z, the pronoun becomes lo/la and the verb loses its final letter: fazer + o gives fazê-lo, and comprar + a gives comprá-la. After a nasal ending (-am, -em, -ão), the pronoun is no/na: Comeram-no. Me, te, nos are also direct objects: Ela me viu.

examples.pt: Eu o vi na loja ontem.
examples.en: I saw him in the shop yesterday.
I want to buy it today.
She invited us to dinner.

lessons.title: Indirect object pronouns: me, te, lhe, nos, lhes
lessons.explanation: The indirect object pronouns are me, te, lhe, nos, lhes (to me, to you, to him/her/you, to us, to them). They replace a + person: Dei o livro a ela becomes Dei-lhe o livro. In writing, lhe is formal and correct for você too. In everyday Brazilian speech, people use te for você, and for the third person they use para ele/ela or a ele/ela: Dei o livro para ela. A gente also uses para + pronoun: Disse para eles. Me and te are shared with the direct object: Ela me deu um presente. Nos is us: Ele nos contou a história.

examples.en: She gave me a present.

examples.pt: Eu te mando uma mensagem hoje.
examples.en: I will send you a message today.
I gave her the book.

lessons.title: Reflexive, reciprocal and pronominal verbs: lavar-se, encontrar-se, esquecer-se
lessons.explanation: Reflexive verbs show that the subject acts on itself: me lavo, te lavas, se lava, nos lavamos, se lavam. The pronouns are me, te, se, nos, se. Reciprocal verbs show an action between people: Eles se abraçaram, Nós nos vemos amanhã. Pronominal verbs always take the pronoun, even if the action is not on oneself: queixar-se, arrepender-se, esquecer-se, lembrar-se, sentar-se. Colloquial Brazilian drops the pronoun with some verbs: Eu esqueci (not Eu me esqueci), but Eu me lembro and Eu me sento keep it. In Brazil the pronoun comes before the verb: Eu me levanto cedo.

lessons.title: Pronoun placement: Brazilian proclisis and formal ênclise
lessons.explanation: In speech and everyday writing, Brazilians put the pronoun before the verb: Me liga, Eu te vi, Ela me disse. With an auxiliary, the pronoun usually goes before the main verb or before the auxiliary: Vou te ligar, Estou te esperando, Não vou me atrasar. Negative words and some adverbs attract the pronoun even in formal Portuguese: Não me diga, Ainda se lembra. Formal writing puts it after the verb with a hyphen (ênclise): Disse-lhe, Diga-me. Never start a formal sentence with an unstressed pronoun: write Diga-me, not Me diga. In speech, Me dá is normal.

examples.en: I will send you the photo now.
